session_name: Hiring, Skills, and Labor Market Dynamics
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Not All That Glitters Is Gold: Firm Hiring in the Market for Knowledge Workers
abstract:
Firms increasingly compete for scientific talent to drive innovation. While individuals' productivity in an industrial setting is uncertain at the time of hire, firms can observe measures of academic productivity. However, because the institutional environments of academia and industry differ, the scientists most productive in academia may not be those most productive in industry. 

Using confidential administrative data on 40 cohorts of PhD graduates across all fields linked to wage and publication records, I estimate individuals' productivity in both academia and industry, regardless of their actual sector of employment. I do so using a Marginal Treatment Effects framework that accounts for endogenous sorting into sectors and exploits variation in industry demand for PhDs at graduation. 

I find that individuals' academic and industrial productivity are only weakly aligned, with an average correlation of 0.29. This alignment has declined by 31% between 1980 and 2010, implying that academic productivity has become a less reliable predictor of industrial productivity over time. This correlation also varies markedly across PhD majors: it is lower in Engineering (0.16 on average) and higher in Social Sciences (0.52 on average). 

In majors with weaker alignment, firms' hires are more likely to be laid off. Specifically, a 0.1 decrease in the correlation is associated with a 19% increase in the layoff rate relative to the mean. This result is consistent with an evaluation challenge with direct implications for hiring outcomes: when academic productivity is a noisier proxy of industrial productivity, firms are more likely to employ individuals whose academic strengths do not translate well to industrial settings, increasing the incidence of false-positive hires. Heterogeneity analyses further suggest that these evaluation challenges are more pronounced for smaller firms and R&D occupations. 

Together, the results suggest that relying on performance indicators generated in a different institutional context can increase organizations’ risk of employing individuals who subsequently underperform.

session_name: Hiring, Skills, and Labor Market Dynamics
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Wilson Martinez Diaz (Carnegie Mellon University); Daniel Stock (Carnegie Mellon University); Erica Fuchs (Carnegie Mellon University); Christophe Combemale (Carnegie Mellon University)
author_names: Martinez Diaz, Wilson*; Stock, Daniel; Fuchs, Erica; Combemale, Christophe
title: Skill-Biased or Skill-Agnostic Hiring? Evidence from the U.S. Semiconductor Industry
abstract: Understanding how firms adjust labor demand in response to industrial policy and technological change is essential for assessing large scale domestic manufacturing feasibility. Initiatives such as the CHIPS and Science Act and the Inflation Reduction Act suggest a period of substantial job creation and increased risk of labor displacement. Whether the United States can build sufficient industrial capacity under these conditions depends on how firms respond to market thinness induced skill shortages, and policy induced shocks. In this paper, we examine hiring behavior in the U.S. semiconductor industry following the $50 billion CHIPS and Science Act. We ask whether firms facing expansion adopt skill-agnostic or skill-biased hiring strategies, whether they prioritize or relax specific skill requirements, and the extent these patterns vary across firm types. While existing literature documents that worker transitions are often costly and uneven, it provides limited evidence on how firms adapt skill requirements in practice. We address this gap by comparing the skill profiles of incumbent occupations and of newly hired workers, where new hires are identified using data from Lightcast. We construct a population-weighted skill profile by integrating OEWS and O*NET data, and identify occupation-specific specialized skills relative to the population baseline. Then, we assess whether the skill magnitude of new hires for those specialized skills more closely resembles incumbents, the general population, or falls in between. This framework provides a systematic way to assess whether firm hiring aligns with occupational skill requirements or reflects broader labor market availability.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Redeployment or Hiring? R&D Characteristics, Organizational Capabilities, and Strategic Human Capital Sourcing in Multi-Business Firms
abstract: Industry shocks reallocate profitability across business units, often forcing multi-business firms to reconfigure their human capital. When a focal business unit experiences a sudden growth inducement, should the firm redeploy employees from other units or hire externally? I develop a task-resource matching view in which sourcing decisions reflect not only transaction and adjustment costs but also the benefits of aligning an employee’s knowledge with task requirements. I study inventor (i.e., engineers and scientists) inflows to ethylene-related business units of petrochemical firms after the U.S. shale revolution, which sharply lowered ethane input costs and increased U.S. ethylene margins beginning in 2011. Using LinkedIn career histories linked to patent records, I observe inventors entering ethylene units of large petrochemical firms (2011-2015) and classify their tasks as downstream new application development or upstream operational efficiency. Consistent with the matching view, firms are more likely to hire externally for new application development roles but rely more on internal redeployment for operational efficiency roles, even after accounting for local hiring frictions and within-firm task relatedness. In addition, these task-contingent patterns are weaker in firms with stronger knowledge recombination capability and more clustered intrafirm inventor networks, suggesting substitution between external hiring and internal knowledge generation/coordination capacities. Additional tests show that external hires bring more novel prior-task knowledge and that performance is highest when the sourcing mode matches task type.

session_name: Hiring, Skills, and Labor Market Dynamics
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Rohan Sharma (The University of British Columbia); Wouter Bam (The University of British Columbia)
title: Skill-Based Measures of Workforce Readiness Across Canadian Regions
abstract:
Assessing whether regions possess the workforce capabilities needed to support industrial change is a central concern for policymakers, firms, and regional development organizations. Existing research has examined labor mobility, firm behavior, and responses to specific demand shocks, but such approaches are often difficult to use as general, ex ante diagnostics for regional strategy. This paper introduces a capability-based framework for measuring regional workforce readiness using occupational skill proximity.
The method combines occupation-level skill profiles with regional occupational employment data to construct employment-weighted regional skill endowments and assess their alignment with the requirements of a target occupation. The resulting readiness measure captures latent occupational capacity embedded in existing workforce composition rather than predicted transitions, wages, or job creation. Conceptually, the framework treats labor as a stock of capabilities shaped by past economic activity, providing insight into what regions are structurally prepared to support.
Building on prior task and skill-based analyses of labor markets, including recent work in the US context, the approach emphasizes interpretability, transferability, and consistent comparison across places. Applied across Canadian urban regions using harmonized occupational employment and standardized skill information, the framework enables systematic assessment of workforce readiness across cities. An illustrative application shows that readiness changes with the skill threshold used, yielding a broad set of possible occupational options at lower thresholds and a smaller set of closely related occupations that are more realistic candidates for targeted training at higher thresholds.
For policymakers and regional development practitioners, the framework offers a practical tool to align workforce development strategies with realistic, place-based industrial opportunities. More broadly, the paper contributes to industry studies by reframing labor as a stock of capabilities that shapes feasible paths of regional transformation.

session_name: Platform Work, Control, and Worker Voice
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Avner Ben-Ner (Carlson School of Management, University of Minnesota); Andrew Weaver (University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign); Ainhoa Urtasun (Public University of Navarra); Adrianto Adrianto (Ministry of Finance)
author_names: Ben-Ner, Avner*; Weaver, Andrew; Urtasun, Ainhoa; Adrianto, Adrianto
title: The Impact of Robotics on the Demand for Skills
abstract:
Recent firm-level difference-in-differences studies across multiple countries find that robot-adopting firms often experience net employment gains, driven by output expansion that outweighs direct task automation. While this literature has substantially advanced our understanding of employment effects, far less is known about how robot adoption reshapes the demand for skills within and across occupations. Existing evidence suggests that robots substitute for routine tasks while increasing demand for complementary activities such as monitoring, maintenance, logistics, and quality control, leading to occupational reallocation and skill upgrading among both production and technical workers.
This paper investigates how robot adoption affects a broad set of skills across multiple occupations at the plant level. We conceptualize robots as transforming task requirements not only within the robotized stage of production, but also across upstream and downstream production stages and support functions. As a result, robot adoption may induce skill changes that extend beyond directly automated tasks, altering the overall skill profile of establishments.
Empirically, we combine detailed job-posting data from Lightcast covering U.S. manufacturing establishments between 2010 and 2025 with plant-level measures of robot adoption. Job postings allow us to observe changes in demanded skills at a granular level, including technical, cognitive, digital, and coordination-related competencies. Using an event-study difference-in-differences framework, we estimate how robot adoption affects skill demand overall and within specific occupations.
Our findings provide new evidence on the skill consequences of industrial automation, highlighting how robots reconfigure human work inside and beyond the production line. The results contribute to debates on technological change, workforce adjustment, and the distributional consequences of automation.

session_name: AI, Technology, and the Changing Nature of Work
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Hun Whee Lee (The Ohio State University); Christopher  Dishop (Auburn University); Nai-Wen Chi (National Sun Yat-Sen University); Yonghwan 	Lee (Kyungpook National University); Wu Wei (Wuhan University); Ke Michael Mai (China Europe International Business School)
author_names: Lee, Hun Whee*; Dishop, Christopher ; Chi, Nai-Wen; 	Lee, Yonghwan; Wei, Wu; Mai, Ke Michael
author_emails: lee.7313@osu.edu*; cdishop@auburn.edu; nwchi@mail.nsysu.edu.tw; yonghwan.lee@mail.mcgill.ca; weiwumail@163.com; kemai@ceibs.edu
title: When Age Helps or Hinders AI Use: A Goal Orientation and Appraisal Perspective
abstract:
As organizations race to embed artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday work, a popular belief is that older employees are less likely to adopt and use AI tools—a belief that can shape staffing decisions, access to advanced training, and whose expertise is leveraged during digital transformation. We examine this assumption in a high-stakes setting: high-tech industries in Taiwan, where participating firms were rapidly pursuing AI-enabled digital transformation and actively encouraging employees to integrate AI into daily work. In such contexts, the “AI is for the young” narrative is especially consequential because it can sideline experienced employees precisely when organizations need broad-based adoption to realize returns on AI investments. At the same time, emerging perspectives suggest that the belief is not only empirically fragile but also theoretically misguided: older workers may bring deep experiential knowledge and strategic thinking that can support technology use and innovation (Baltes & Smith, 2003; Chang et al., 2023; Gallistl et al., 2024; Ng & Feldman, 2013), challenging age-essentialist accounts that portray older employees as inherently less adaptable to AI-era demands (Case, 2024; Paradis, 2024; Timis, 2025).

Rather than asking whether older workers can use AI, we ask when age functions as a motivational asset versus a liability for AI use (defined as the extent to which employees integrate AI tools into their work activities). Drawing on goal orientation theory (Dweck, 1986; VandeWalle, 1997) and the challenge–hindrance appraisal framework (Cavanaugh et al., 2000; LePine et al., 2005), we propose a motivational appraisal model in which age relates to AI use indirectly through employees’ appraisals of AI as a challenge (a mastery opportunity) versus a hindrance (a disruptive constraint). We argue that goal orientations shape these appraisals: older employees high in learning goal orientation (LGO) should be more likely to frame AI as a developmental challenge and less likely to experience it as a hindrance (Kozlowski et al., 2001; Payne et al., 2007), whereas older employees high in performance-avoid goal orientation (PAGO) may disengage by perceiving AI as threatening established routines and competence (Elliot & Harackiewicz, 1996; Ferris et al., 2013).

This research makes two primary contributions. First, it challenges deficit-based assumptions about older workers and AI by offering a boundary-condition account of when and why age supports versus constrains AI use, helping to counter stereotypes and the organizational risks of age-based stigmatization (Henkens, 2005; Posthuma & Campion, 2009; Posthuma et al., 2012). Second, while prior work has largely emphasized downstream consequences of AI use for creativity, performance, and productivity (Boussioux et al., 2024; Jia et al., 2024; Noy & Zhang, 2023; Senoner et al., 2024; Shin et al., 2023; Su et al., 2024), we illuminate motivational antecedents—an approach well-suited to a domain that demands self-regulation, error tolerance, and sustained learning (Dahri et al., 2024; Lan & Zhou, 2025). Practically, the results suggest that inclusive AI transformation requires more than access and encouragement: organizations can better mobilize experienced talent by cultivating learning-oriented climates and developmental framing that help employees—especially older employees—interpret AI as an opportunity for mastery rather than a hindrance.

session_name: AI, Technology, and the Changing Nature of Work
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Driving the Skill Shift: The Impact of Generative AI Adoption on Skill Demand in the Labor Market
abstract: The rapid diffusion of generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping organizational practices and labor market dynamics, yet the mechanisms through which these transformations unfold remain poorly understood. While prior research has emphasized the automation and augmentation effects of AI technologies, far less is known about how GenAI transforms firms’ skill requirements. This study addresses this gap by providing causal evidence on how GenAI adoption reshapes firm-level skill demand through the lens of AI literacy. We construct a large-scale firm–quarter panel of U.S. public firms from 2021 to 2025 by integrating 10-K filings and conference call transcripts. Using large language models, we classify firms into GenAI adopters (i.e., firms that adopt generative AI), AI-only adopters (i.e., firms that adopt traditional AI but not generative AI), and Non-adopters (i.e., firms that adopt neither traditional AI nor generative AI). We then combine this classification with over 113 million job postings and measure firm-level skill demand using a taxonomy of technical, evaluation, and human skills derived from the AI literacy framework. To identify causal effects, we employ a staggered difference-in-differences design. We find that, relative to Non-adopters, GenAI adoption increases demand for all three skill categories. However, when compared to AI-only adopters, GenAI adoption generates significant increases in evaluation and human skills, while technical skill demand does not increase significantly. These patterns indicate that the marginal impact of GenAI lies in higher-order cognitive and interactive capabilities rather than in additional technical proficiencies. Split-sample analyses further show that these effects are concentrated in knowledge-intensive industries. Overall, the findings identify GenAI as a qualitatively distinct and more transformative technological shock to labor market than prior generations of AI. The study contributes to the literature on AI and the future of work, and offer actionable guidance for firms, educators, and policymakers in designing workforce development strategies.

session_name: AI, Technology, and the Changing Nature of Work
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Designing industrial policy to create good jobs in an age of AI: Suggestions from history
abstract:
A “good jobs” or “high road” strategy promotes both equity and efficiency. In this strategy, highly-skilled workers make innovative and sustainable products ; their productivity enables high wages for workers, good products for consumers, and fair profits for managers, while promoting a clean environment.  (See for example books by Paul Osterman; Zeynep Ton; articles by Helper 2009; Luria and Rogers).
Over the past 40 years, there have been a variety of efforts to build on new technologies and managerial practices to achieve  good jobs, including CNC machining; lean production; flexible automation; smart manufacturing, and now AI.  This high road model has long been proposed (including by me), but has only rarely been adopted in the US.  
The difficulty of adoption has been (at least) two-fold: First, the high road (or “ good jobs strategy”  works only if a company adopts several practices at the same time. It must improve communication skills at all levels, create mechanisms for communicating new ideas across a supply chains levels and functions, and provide incentives to use them. Merely getting the prices right (adding taxes or subsidies to correct for market failures) is not sufficient to build these capabilities. Instead, it makes sense to provide technical assistance services to firms directly, and to develop eco-systems of collaborative supplier relations, patient capital  -- not just siloed workforce training efforts. 
Second, many of the benefits of the high-road strategy accrue to workers, suppliers, and communities in the form of higher wages and more stable employment. Profit-maximizing firms do not take these benefits into account when deciding, for example, how much to invest in training. Many firms will provide less than the socially optimal amount of general training because they fear trained employees will be hired away by other firms
 This paper (a draft chapter of a book I’m writing) will explore a variety of examples of efforts to create good jobs. It will draw on a variety of interviews and plant visits I’ve conducted over the past several decades in the industry studies tradition.   Today we again have a new technology in the works, artificial intelligence, that some argue could be used to augment worker capabilities and bring a new era of abundance and prosperity for all.  The paper will draw suggestions from these past technology and management innovations to provide suggestions for managers and public policymakers about how to design strategies that might make this promise more of a reality.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Athar Mansoor (University of Cambridge); Eoin O' Sullivan (University of Cambridge)
title: Emerging Manufacturing Technologies and the Valley of Death: Skilling Innovation Workforce
abstract:
The journey of an emerging manufacturing technology from initial conception to adoption is fraught with multiple challenges. A significant barrier during this complex odyssey is the Valley of Death (VoD) – a metaphorical chasm representing the problems in translating promising research findings into commercially viable products. Literature has recognized the importance of skilled innovation workforce as a catalyst for successful commercialization and a vital bridge across the VoD. Despite a rising interest in the development of innovation workforce, there is a dearth of research scholarship exploring what types and range of skills are needed for a future ready innovation workforce operating in the VoD. The problem becomes more pronounced from the perspective of emerging manufacturing technologies workforce active within the VoD. Hence, the challenges for diffusion and adoption of emerging manufacturing technologies have increased many times.  
Skilling of emerging technologies workforce has been discussed in the relevant streams of literature i.e., innovation systems, emerging technologies, higher education and absorptive capacity. This research through a mixed-methods approach, therefore, investigates the level of engagement among the aforementioned four strands of scholarship. Our hypothesis is that the four domains do not engage with each other, thereby disconnecting important findings for developing skilled innovation workforce for successful management of complex emerging manufacturing technologies through the VoD. Through a bibliometric analysis and systematic literature review we test our hypothesis to identify the level of connection/disconnection between the related strands of literature and propose policy interventions to reduce gaps between research and industry for developing a futuristic skilled innovation workforce for emerging manufacturing technologies. 
The research objectives include: (1) Identifying the critical skills and competencies required for technology transfer and commercialization in the context of emerging manufacturing technologies. (2) Analyzing the role of a skilled innovation workforce in bridging the gap between R&D and market deployment. (3) Developing a conceptual framework that illustrates the relationship between a skilled workforce, technology transfer, absorptive capacity, commercialization, and innovation policy.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Brian Dan-Ding (Institute for Sound Public Policy/Rutgers University)
title: How U.S. Semiconductor Firms Created an Engineering Labor Shortage and How to Fix It By Bringing Back Workforce Reinvestment
abstract: This research and policy report surveys the research over the last several decades on how the U.S. semiconductor engineering workforce was built up in the 20th century and how it was disinvested in the 21st century. The report additionally analyzed workforce data from the top seven U.S. semiconductor companies (comprising 82% of U.S. semiconductor sales in 2021) and government sources. The report argues that an important under-discussed reason why the industry fell behind in the first place is that American semiconductor companies disinvested in their American workforce by offshoring white-collar jobs, disproportionately laying off Americans, hiring guest workers (including H-1B and Optional Practical Training (OPT) workers, and disinvesting in American engineers and education in the 21st century. Meanwhile, semiconductor companies claimed an engineering labor shortage in the 2000s to advocate for the retention of international students through expanding guest worker programs such as STEM OPT, while pulling back on investing in advanced semiconductor education. Additionally, qualitative interviews with eight current and former American semiconductor engineers supplemented the historical analysis.  The interviews revealed experienced American engineers who were attracted to the industry through employer education incentives, training, and retention programs that produced a stable early to mid-career for them.  Additionally, the government played a key role in providing veterans with the educational opportunity to shift into the industry with the GI Bill. These careers were disrupted because of permanent layoffs firms committed to, along with a shrinking quantity and quality of jobs for industry engineering professionals.  21st-century disinvestment practices diverged from past successful American workforce initiatives that firms undertook, such as raising salaries during engineer shortages and developing retention, recruitment, and education programs. Workforce decisions made by U.S. semiconductor firms were detrimental not just to American professional workers but also to U.S. firms and the United States. The solution for the industry is that the engineering labor market needs to be tightened by reducing the number of white-collar guest work permits in order for semiconductor employers to bring back financial incentives, as they’ve done in the past, to attract American STEM students and workers to the industry. Government policy should safeguard defense and leading-edge semiconductor jobs and prioritize the needs of American workers by reinvigorating the military veteran to semiconductor industry professional pipeline.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Jillian Miles (Carnegie Mellon University); Christophe Combemale (Carnegie Mellon University); Valerie Karplus (Carnegie Mellon University)
author_names: Miles, Jillian*; Combemale, Christophe; Karplus, Valerie
title: Assessing Workforce Readiness for Electric Vehicle Battery Manufacturing Plants in the U.S.
abstract: Investment in electric vehicle (EV) and associated battery manufacturing has increased sharply in the past decade, driven by plans for new large-scale gigafactory-sized facilities. Despite the scale of these development plans, the workforce readiness of candidate geographies remains poorly understood. This study estimates the technical labor makeup of large-scale EV battery manufacturing facilities at the occupation level, and assesses extent to which local labor markets in the continental U.S.  are positioned to absorb one of those facilities. We suggest a new method for estimating plant occupational makeups from resume data and advance skills-matching heuristics by using real-world occupational transition data to inform our assumptions Our findings suggest at least two distinct labor models for EV battery manufacturing facilities, one engineering-intensive, and one more labor-intensive. Metropolitan areas, the Rust Belt, and the “Battery Belt” in the Southeast U.S. exhibit a lower level of labor supply strain than the rest of the country, indicating greater potential to fill plant employment locally. Additionally, we identify that industrial engineers are a bottleneck occupation regardless of geography or plant type, and existing announced locations for gigafactories vary substantially in their baseline workforce readiness. Together, these findings highlight the importance of considering labor availability into industrial siting decisions and suggest a role for targeted workforce and industrial policy to improve alignment between manufacturing investments and local labor markets.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Sun Kim (Michigan State University); Sriram Narayanan (Michigan State University); Ranjan Mukherjee (Michigan State University); Rajiv Ranganathan (Michigan State University); Hung Jen Kuo (Michigan State University)
author_names: Kim, Sun*; Narayanan, Sriram; Mukherjee, Ranjan; Ranganathan, Rajiv; Kuo, Hung Jen
title: Ability-centric Worker-Task Assignment Framework in Apparel Manufacturing
abstract:
The transition toward Industry 5.0 calls for human-centric production systems that embrace workforce diversity rather than treating it as variability to be minimized. This shift is increasingly urgent as firms draw on broader labor pools, including people with disabilities, to address labor market challenges. Yet traditional operations management approaches often rely on aggregated worker categorizations, such as disability status or skill levels, that compress multidimensional ability profiles and obscure task-relevant strengths.
This paper introduces an ability-centric framework for worker-task assignment that moves beyond deficit-based perspectives to embrace a strength-based approach. We represent both workers and tasks along the same ability dimensions - workers as vectors of ability levels and tasks as vectors of ability loads that quantify how sensitive processing times are to each ability (i.e., importance of each ability in task performance). This shared representation makes worker-task fit explicit, enabling assignment decisions based on dimensional alignment of abilities on a granular level. 
We examine this framework in collaboration with Peckham, Inc., a vocational rehabilitation organization operating garment production lines where approximately 75% of workers have disabilities. Using a bi-objective optimization model that balances productivity and fairness simultaneously, we trace how these outcomes move together as emphasis on each objective changes. 
Our analysis reveals the following key insights. First, we show that representing tasks and workers at a granular ability level makes worker-task fit visible and actionable. By quantifying abilities of workers and tasks as vectors, the framework provides a foundation to match workers to tasks where they are most likely to succeed based on their specific strengths and the alignment of those strengths to what a task requires. This operationalizes a strength-based approach that echoes Henry Ford’s insight that not all tasks require full physical capacity, and workers with limited abilities can perform well when assigned to tasks that align with their specific ability profile.
Second, through bi-objective optimization, we show a nonlinear efficiency-fairness trade-off relationship. We find that considering fairness in line optimization can improve fairness (i.e., even distribution of workloads across workers) with a modest decrease in productivity. More importantly, as the system places higher emphasis on fairness, it introduces a significant increase in systemic flexibility as a byproduct, measured by the number of workers who can be assigned. The framework leverages task-specific ability requirements to allow the line to integrate diverse ability profiles.
Third, this framework introduces significant opportunities for practice by providing a clear pathway for workforce management, such as targeted training to improve workers’ capability and career advancement that contribute to performance improvement and workplace well-being. Moreover, on a line-level, it enables line managers to identify which specific ability dimension is driving a bottleneck. By pinpointing whether a workstation is slowed by an ability misalignment or an a specific ability’s overload, management can plan targeted augmentations such as assistive technology or task redesign.

session_name: Platform Work, Control, and Worker Voice
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Alex Kowalski (Cornell ILR School); Erin Kelly (MIT Sloan School of Management); Hazhir Rahmandad (MIT Sloan School of Management); Kirsten Siebach (Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health)
author_names: Kowalski, Alex*; Kelly, Erin; Rahmandad, Hazhir; Siebach, Kirsten
title: Can a voice channel reduce turnover? Evidence on employee voice and exit from a cluster-randomized trial in U.S. fulfillment centers
abstract: Building on the long research tradition on employee voice and its impact on both employees and organizations, we investigate whether a new voice channel reduces job exit in e-commerce fulfillment centers. A cluster-randomized trial compared hourly workers in sites randomized to launch the voice channel (Health and Well-Being Committees, or HaWCs) with those employed by the same U.S. firm in control sites. This participatory intervention involved a small group of frontline workers and supervisors who solicited concerns and ideas about workplace stressors, work processes, and safety from the broader workforce and then developed and implemented improvement projects in respon0se. HaWCs were an isolated change, rather than one component of a high-involvement work system, and they were implemented in non-union workplaces, raising questions about their likely impact. An intention-to-treat analysis finds individual workers’ monthly probability of exit fell by 1.3%-points in HaWC sites in the year after randomization, representing a 19.7% decline relative to pre-intervention exit rates. Two secondary analyses show that exit risk is significantly lower for workers in sites where more workplace improvements are made and among individuals who attribute more improvements to the HaWCs. Our findings demonstrate the feasibility of addressing turnover and improving the work environment with employee voice, even in tough conditions like fulfillment centers. They also highlight the ways in which the opportunity to voice and the impact voice has on work conditions are holistically related to turnover while underscoring the importance of separating voice channels from supporting structures and practices when estimating voice effects.

session_name: Platform Work, Control, and Worker Voice
category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Yi-Su Chen (University of Michigan - Dearborn); Yinyin Cao (University of Michigan - Dearborn); Kang Hsu (Florida Gulf Coast University)
author_names: Chen, Yi-Su; Cao, Yinyin*; Hsu, Kang
title: Should we judge a book by its cover? The role of artists as content suppliers in new board game development
abstract:
Research on new product development (NPD) in operations and supply chain management has largely focused on mature manufacturing industries characterized by long-term buyer-supplier relationships and a strong emphasis on cost and efficiency-based performance criteria. In contrast to these conventional supply chains, NPD projects in creative industries often occur through collaborations that extend beyond the traditional boundaries of the firm. Many of these collaborations involve supplying firms or individuals who operate as freelance suppliers and contribute on a project-by-project basis, reflecting the increasing prevalence of temporary forms of work (Samimi & Sydow, 2021).

In this study, we explore supplier selection in board game development, a setting within the cultural and creative industries, where suppliers are individual freelancers who work on NPD projects based on short-term contractual relationships. The board game industry offers a unique lens to study innovation, as consumers engage with the products not for utilitarian value, but rather for fun and enjoyment. Further, consumer tastes are diverse and constantly evolving, thus requiring suppliers to continuously experiment to create novel outcomes that may appeal to unpredictable consumer preferences (Potts et al., 2008). 

We focus in this study on artists and their impact on a game’s aesthetic performance, as captured by both aesthetic novelty and aesthetic appeal. Following existing NPD research that has emphasized the importance of skills and network ties in supplier selection (e.g., Lawson et al., 2015; Yan et al., 2020), our study is guided by the following research questions: (1) How does the breadth of an artist’s aesthetic knowledge influence a board game’s performance? and (2) How do artists’ network positionings moderate the relationship between their aesthetic diversity and board game performance?    

To answer our research questions, we develop hypotheses using frameworks from human capital and social capital theories. Using data retrieved from the BoardGameGeek website, we find that the diversity of an artist’s aesthetic portfolio is positively related to both the aesthetic novelty and appeal of a board game. An artist’s network positioning, on the other hand, has more nuanced effects: not only do different network centralities (as captured via degree centrality, betweenness centrality, and eigenvector centrality) have opposing effects on a particular measure of game performance, but the same network centrality may also have opposing effects on different measures of game performance. This suggests that having more direct ties as well as occupying an important network position can be a double-edged sword for a diverse artist. Our examination of freelance suppliers within an innovation-driven, project-based industry such as board games extends the interorganizational NPD literature that has primarily focused on more stable buyer-supplier relationships in mature industries, and offers insights on supplier selection in a context of high market uncertainty.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Manuel Torres-Sahli (Universidad De Los Andes, Chile); Alfredo Enrione (Ese Business School, Universidad De Los Andes, Chile); Santiago Truffa (Universidad Adolfo Ibañez, Chile); Felipe Aldunate (Ese Business School, Universidad De Los Andes, Chile); Jacinta Girardi (Buk, Chile); Constanza Opazo (Buk, Chile)
author_names: Torres-Sahli, Manuel*; Enrione, Alfredo; Truffa, Santiago; Aldunate, Felipe; Girardi, Jacinta; Opazo, Constanza
author_emails: mtorressahli@gmail.com*; aenrione.ese@uandes.cl; santiago.truffa@uai.cl; faldunate.ese@uandes.cl; jgirardi@buk.cl; copazo@buk.cl
title: Hierarchies: New Facts from Administrative HR Data
abstract:
How do firms construct internal hierarchies, and how do these structures shape compensation, turnover, and opportunity across industries? Despite the central role of hierarchy in organizational theory, direct empirical evidence has been constrained by data that typically infer reporting relationships from job titles or observe only top executives. We address this gap using administrative data from a human resources platform that directly records reporting relationships for all employees—from CEOs to frontline workers—linked to compensation, turnover, absences, and team structure across 247 firms and 1.4 million employee-months.

We document several stylized facts with implications for understanding industry dynamics and internal labor markets. First, hierarchy height varies substantially even among similarly sized firms: each doubling of firm size adds only 0.5 layers on average, suggesting that organizational depth reflects strategic choice rather than mechanical scaling. Second, compensation is sharply convex in hierarchical position: CEO-to-median pay ratios rise from 3× in three-layer firms to 7× in six-layer firms, with approximately 75% of wage variation occurring within rather than between firms. Third, hierarchy predicts worker behavior: lower-level positions exhibit significantly higher turnover, and within-team wage inequality amplifies exit even after controlling for individual wages. Fourth, women comprise only 11–12% of top-level positions despite representing 39% of the workforce—a gap that persists within firms and industries.

Most relevant for industry studies, we find that the relationship between firm size and hierarchical depth varies markedly across industries. Professional services add nearly one full layer per doubling of firm size (elasticity: 1.07), while hospitality adds less than half a layer (elasticity: 0.38). Knowledge-intensive industries—professional services, finance, information technology—exhibit steeper hierarchical scaling than industries with more standardized production processes. These cross-industry differences suggest that organizational design responds systematically to industry-specific coordination demands, production technologies, and labor market conditions.

The current analysis draws on approximately 10% of firms available through the platform. Ongoing data expansion will scale the sample to over 2,000 firms and 14 million employee-months, enabling finer-grained industry and firm-size comparisons. The patterns documented here provide preliminary empirical benchmarks for theories of organizational structure, incentives, and internal labor markets—and highlight the value of administrative organizational data for understanding how industry characteristics shape the internal architecture of firms.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Do Managers Capture Firm Surplus? Evidence from Human Capital Development and Residual Profits
abstract:
Strategy research has largely viewed human capital development through the lens of value creation. This study examines how human capital development also shapes employees’ value-appropriation process, with particular attention to how internally developed, firm-specific, and co-specialized skills alter bargaining dynamics between firms and workers. Drawing on the New Stakeholder Theory (NST) and the Resource-Based View (RBV), the study argues that while co-specialized human capital enhances value creation by embedding individual skills within firm-specific resources, routines, and coordination mechanisms, it simultaneously constrains employees’ ability to capture a proportional share of the value they help generate. In this sense, human capital development is not only a source of competitive advantage but also a mechanism that reshapes stakeholder claims on value.
Using longitudinal panel data from the Human Capital Corporate Panel (HCCP) in South Korea (2009-2017 bi-annually), this study analyzes how firm-level excess operating income (operationalized as residual isolated from regressing expected EBIT) translates into individual wages, focusing primarily on managers as a critical internal stakeholder group. By linking within-firm surplus shocks to individual-level compensation outcomes, the study directly examines value appropriation at the employee level, where both human capital development and rent distribution can be observed. The analysis further distinguishes between different human capital development pathways, including firm-guided and approved training, and collective in-house training (e.g., form of interactions among workers) as key mechanisms through which co-specialization emerges.
The results indicate that firm-level surplus is not fully captured by managers, despite their central role in value creation and their deep embeddedness in organizational processes. The extent to which firm surplus is reflected in managerial compensation hinges on how managers’ human capital is developed. When skill development occurs under firm-guided and approved training, the relationship between firm-level surplus and managerial wages is significantly weakened, suggesting limited value capture by managers. However, under conditions of intensive firm investment in human capital, such as greater overall training intensity, this weakening effect may be partially attenuated. Overall, the findings suggest that human capital development shapes not only value creation but also the distribution of value among internal stakeholders, which emphasizes the role of co-specialization as a rent-retention mechanism for firms rather than a rent-sharing mechanism for employees.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: The Institutional Economics of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Higher Education: A Transaction Cost Analysis of University Transformation
abstract:
Why do universities persist in their current bundled form - integrating research, teaching, credentialing, and socialization within hierarchical organizations - when alternative arrangements for knowledge production and transmission have proliferated? This paper applies transaction cost economics (TCE) to answer this question and to analyze how artificial intelligence (AI) may fundamentally transform the institutional logic of higher education. While canonical organization theories describe how universities function internally - as loosely coupled systems (Weick, 1976), legitimacy-seeking entities (Meyer & Rowan, 1977), or organized anarchies (Cohen, March, & Olsen, 1972) - they do not explain why the bundled form emerged and persists. TCE provides this foundation (Coase, 1937; Williamson, 1985), demonstrating that universities internalize functions whose coordination through markets would be prohibitively costly due to verification challenges, monitoring difficulties, appropriability problems (Teece, 1986), and the tacit nature of professional knowledge transfer (Polanyi, 1966).

The paper makes three contributions to organization theory. First, it extends TCE into higher education, developing a systematic account of why credentialing solves signaling problems in labor markets characterized by information asymmetry (Spence, 1973; Akerlof, 1970), why instruction addresses monitoring challenges that market-based provision cannot resolve (Nelson, 1970), why research bundling enables knowledge appropriation under weak intellectual property conditions (Arrow, 1962; Teece, 1986), and why socialization transfers tacit expertise that resists market coordination (Lave & Wenger, 1991). Second, and more fundamentally, the paper advances transaction cost theory by distinguishing between marginal and parametric technological effects on governance structures. Prior technologies - printing, broadcasting, the internet - produced marginal effects: they reduced certain transaction costs while leaving the fundamental parameters that favor bundled governance intact. This explains why universities absorbed these technologies without institutional displacement, and why MOOCs failed to disrupt traditional institutions despite initial predictions (Hoxby, 2014; Reich & Ruipérez-Valiente, 2019). Artificial intelligence differs because it transforms the parameters themselves. AI does not merely make monitoring cheaper; it changes what monitoring means when human and machine contributions become indistinguishable (Cotton, Cotton, & Shipway, 2023). AI does not simply reduce information asymmetry; it creates new forms of asymmetry regarding algorithmic processes while dissolving traditional asymmetries regarding expert knowledge (Agrawal, Gans, & Goldfarb, 2018).

Third, the paper integrates TCE with institutional theory (DiMaggio & Powell, 1983) to explain organizational persistence and change under technological disruption. The analysis yields a typology that maps university functions according to AI substitutability and verification complexity, generating propositions about which institutional arrangements face displacement (content delivery, routine assessment), which gain distinctive importance (professional identity formation, ethical development, research apprenticeship), and which become contested terrain where institutions and markets compete on verification capacity (complex skill development, collaborative capabilities). The framework provides principled criteria for distinguishing between functions that remain essential - continuing to solve transaction cost problems AI does not address - and those that are historically contingent, persisting only through legitimacy and inertia.

For industry studies scholars, this paper demonstrates how transaction cost analysis can illuminate institutional transformation in knowledge-intensive industries facing technological disruption. The distinction between marginal and parametric technological effects has implications far beyond higher education, providing theoretical grounding for understanding why some technologies produce incremental adaptation while others precipitate genuine institutional transformation (Langlois, 2003). For policymakers navigating AI's impact on the higher education industry, the framework offers tools for anticipating which institutional arrangements will prove durable and which require fundamental reconceptualization - a question of considerable consequence as institutions, employers, and governments grapple with AI's implications for workforce development, credentialing, and knowledge production.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
title: Climate Smart Staffing for Harvest Management
abstract:
The U.S. tree fruit industry, valued at $34.2 billion, faces a crisis as labor costs in Washington’s apple sector rose from 37% to 99% of grower returns between 2013 and 2023. Climate change exacerbates this by shifting harvest windows, complicating the management of local and immigrant (H-2A) labor pools.

This research proposes a dynamic planning engine using Stochastic Dynamic Programming (SDP) and Distributionally Robust Optimization (DRO) to optimize labor acquisition and scheduling under coupled weather and workforce uncertainties. Unlike existing literature, this model addresses tail-risk events like heatwaves and explores responsible scheduling to improve local labor outcomes.

Key findings and contributions include the following key aspects. First, improving profitability by utilizing adaptive hiring strategies that can increase profits by up to 27%. Second, on policy reform, reducing the 90-day H-2A lead time can generate cost savings of 6% to 17%, providing a quantitative basis for visa reform. Third, on risk hedging, the framework establishes thresholds for harvest window overlaps between states, identifying when operational mitigation must be supplemented by financial insurance. Finally, on labor participation, clustering idle weeks can improve structured scheduling by 78%, allowing local workers to pursue supplemental employment.

By integrating physical system dynamics with operational implementation, this engine enables growers to secure high-margin revenue through precise, time-sensitive harvesting while navigating modern climate and regulatory frictions.

category: Labor Markets, Organizations, and the Future of Work
authors: Ron Hira (Howard University); Hal Salzman (Rutgers University)
title: Forecasting the Winners and Losers of H-1B Reforms Across Industries and Workers: Will firms, universities, and health care lose workers or profits?
abstract: As the U.S.’s largest skilled guestworker program, the H-1B visa is used by tens of thousands of firms who employ more than 600 thousand of these guestworkers. The H-1B program has been described as the swiss army knife of guest worker programs because of the varied nature of employers and workers who use it. The Trump administration proposing the most farreaching reforms to the H-1B program since its inception. The three reforms implemented for this year are: 1) employers are assessed a new $100,000 fee for visas for certain workers, 2) the annual process for selecting new visas has been modified to favor higher wages, and 3) stepped up enforcement of program rules by the Department of Labor (DOL) . The DOL has also announced changes the minimum wage employers are required to pay H-1B workers. These reforms will alter the types of firms that apply for and receive visas, and the pool of worker-beneficiaries. We examine the expected winners and losers from these policy changes and potential impact, with focus  on the tech sector as the largest user of this guestworker visa and health care system which relies on the H-1B for a large supply of residents.
